# From records to relationships {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Most data we've seen looks like this

| customer | age | city | spend |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 34 | DC | 120 |
| B | 28 | NYC | 85 |
| C | 41 | DC | 230 |

Rows = independent observations. Columns = variables.

**Every chart so far has assumed the rows are independent of one another.**

## But much of the world's most interesting data is *relational*

- Who follows whom · who emails whom
- Papers citing papers · proteins interacting
- **Web pages linking to web pages** — the graph search engines are built on
- Money flowing between accounts
- Roads connecting intersections

::: {.gw-box}
A table can store this, but it cannot show it. The information is in the connections, which needs a different data structure and a different set of visual conventions.
:::

## The network view

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx

G = nx.karate_club_graph()
pos = nx.spring_layout(G, seed=42)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, ax=ax, with_labels=False,
                 node_color="#2E6E8E", node_size=120,
                 edge_color="#bbbbbb")
ax.set_title("Zachary's Karate Club — 34 people, 78 friendships", fontsize=11)
ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
The classic example: a university karate club that famously split into two factions after a dispute between the instructor and the president. The split is *visible* in the structure — no table of members would show it. We'll use this graph all session.
:::

# Why this became a field {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Two papers, eighteen months apart {.smaller}

Until the late 1990s a network was modelled as one of two things: a **regular lattice**, where every node has the same neighbours, or an **Erdős–Rényi random graph**, where every pair is connected by a coin flip. Real networks are neither.

**Watts & Strogatz (1998)**, *Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks*, [Nature 393:440](https://www.nature.com/articles/30918)

- Take a regular ring, rewire a few edges at random, and path lengths collapse while local clustering survives
- Shown on three unrelated systems: *C. elegans* neurons, the US power grid, and film-actor collaborations

**Barabási & Albert (1999)**, *Emergence of scaling in random networks*, [Science 286:509](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.286.5439.509)

- Networks that **grow**, with new nodes preferring to attach to already-popular ones, develop a power-law degree distribution — a few enormous hubs and a long tail
- Found in the web, citations, and metabolic networks

::: {.gw-box}
Why it mattered: the same structure kept appearing in systems with nothing else in common, which meant one set of tools could be pointed at neurons, power grids, web pages and friendships alike. That is the ground computational social science and much of applied network analysis is built on.
:::

## Three kinds of network {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np

n_draw, k_draw = 40, 4
reg_s = nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n_draw, k_draw, 0.0, seed=1)
rnd_s = nx.gnm_random_graph(n_draw, n_draw * k_draw // 2, seed=1)
rnd_s = rnd_s.subgraph(max(nx.connected_components(rnd_s), key=len)).copy()
sf_s = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n_draw, k_draw // 2, seed=1)

n_big, k_big = 2000, 6
big = [nx.watts_strogatz_graph(n_big, k_big, 0.0, seed=1),
       nx.gnm_random_graph(n_big, n_big * k_big // 2, seed=1),
       nx.barabasi_albert_graph(n_big, k_big // 2, seed=1)]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10.4, 4.3),
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
titles = ["Regular", "Random", "Scale-free"]
layouts = [nx.circular_layout(reg_s), nx.spring_layout(rnd_s, seed=2),
           nx.spring_layout(sf_s, seed=2)]
for ax, Gs, lp, name in zip(axes[0], [reg_s, rnd_s, sf_s], layouts, titles):
    degs = dict(Gs.degree())
    nx.draw_networkx(Gs, lp, ax=ax, with_labels=False, edge_color="#9fb4c0",
                     width=0.9, node_color="#2E6E8E",
                     node_size=[6 + degs[v] * 3 for v in Gs.nodes()])
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11); ax.axis("off")

for ax, Gb in zip(axes[1], big):
    d = [v for _, v in Gb.degree()]
    ax.hist(d, bins=range(0, max(d) + 2), color="#2E6E8E")
    ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlim(0, 60)
    ax.set_xlabel("degree", fontsize=8); ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
axes[1][0].set_ylabel("nodes (log)", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Networks drawn at n = 40; the degree distributions below use n = 2000 so the tail is visible. **Degree** is just the number of edges a node has.

Regular: every node has the same degree, so the distribution is a single spike. Random: degrees cluster around the average and nothing is far from it. Scale-free: most nodes have very few edges and a handful have very many — the shape that produces hubs.

## The small-world result, in numbers {.smaller}

All three have 500 nodes and an average of 6 edges per node. Only the wiring differs.

| | Clustering | Average path | Largest degree |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regular ring | **0.600** | **42.1** | 6 |
| Random | 0.012 | 3.7 | 14 |
| Scale-free | 0.047 | 3.3 | **67** |

A regular ring keeps your neighbours connected but takes 42 steps to cross; a random graph crosses in under 4 but has no local structure. Real social networks have both. Watts and Strogatz rewired a small share of the ring's edges at random:

| Fraction rewired | Clustering | Average path |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | 0.600 | 42.1 |
| 1% | 0.588 | 14.4 |
| **5%** | **0.516** | **6.6** |
| 100% | 0.012 | 3.7 |

::: {.gw-box}
Rewiring one edge in twenty costs 14% of the clustering and removes 84% of the distance. A handful of long-range shortcuts is enough to make a large network small — which is why six degrees of separation is not a paradox.
:::

# Anatomy of a graph {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The vocabulary

- **Node** (vertex): an entity — a person, paper, account, place
- **Edge** (link): a relationship between two nodes
- A **graph** $G = (V, E)$ — a set of nodes and a set of edges. That's it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6))
mini = nx.Graph([("Ana","Ben"),("Ben","Cal"),("Ana","Cal"),("Cal","Dee")])
mpos = nx.spring_layout(mini, seed=3)
nx.draw_networkx(mini, mpos, ax=ax, node_color="#2E6E8E",
                 font_color="white", node_size=1500, font_size=9,
                 edge_color="#888888", width=2)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Edges carry meaning

**Direction** — does the relationship point one way?

- Friendship: usually *undirected*
- "Follows", "cites", "pays": *directed* (arrows matter)

**Weight** — how strong is the tie?

- Number of emails exchanged, dollars transferred, co-occurrences

::: {.gw-box}
Before visualizing any network, ask: **directed or not? weighted or not?** The answers change both the analysis and the drawing.
:::

## What direction and weight look like {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.2))

# --- directed: in-degree and out-degree are different questions ---
D = nx.DiGraph([("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("E", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")])
dpos = nx.spring_layout(D, seed=11)
nx.draw_networkx(D, dpos, ax=axes[0], node_color="#2E6E8E", font_color="white",
                 node_size=900, font_size=9, edge_color="#888888",
                 arrows=True, arrowsize=16, width=1.6)
axes[0].set_title(f"Directed: C has in-degree {D.in_degree('C')}, "
                  f"out-degree {D.out_degree('C')}", fontsize=10)
axes[0].axis("off")

# --- weighted: the tie strength is the data, so it goes on a channel ---
W = nx.Graph()
W.add_weighted_edges_from([("Ana", "Ben", 1), ("Ben", "Cal", 9),
                           ("Ana", "Cal", 3), ("Cal", "Dee", 6)])
wpos = nx.spring_layout(W, seed=3)
nx.draw_networkx(W, wpos, ax=axes[1], node_color="#2E6E8E", font_color="white",
                 node_size=900, font_size=9, edge_color="#888888",
                 width=[W[u][v]["weight"] * 0.6 for u, v in W.edges()])
nx.draw_networkx_edge_labels(W, wpos, ax=axes[1], font_size=8,
                             edge_labels=nx.get_edge_attributes(W, "weight"))
axes[1].set_title("Weighted: edge width carries the strength", fontsize=10)
axes[1].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**Direction** splits degree into two different questions. C is cited by three nodes and cites one, and "who is cited most" and "who cites most" have different answers — `G.in_degree()` and `G.out_degree()` instead of `G.degree()`.

**Weight** is data about the edge, so it needs a channel. Width is the usual choice. Note that most measures accept it: `nx.betweenness_centrality(G, weight="weight")` treats a heavy edge as a *longer* path, which is often the opposite of what you intend — check what your weight means before passing it.

## The same graph, two representations {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 4.2))
nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, ax=ax, with_labels=False,
                 node_color="#2E6E8E", node_size=80, edge_color="#cccccc")
ax.set_title("Node–link diagram", fontsize=11)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np
A = nx.to_numpy_array(G)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.8, 4.2))
ax.imshow(A, cmap="Blues")
ax.set_title("Adjacency matrix", fontsize=11)
ax.set_xlabel("node j"); ax.set_ylabel("node i")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::
::::

Same 78 edges. $A_{ij}=1$ when an edge connects $i$ and $j$. The node–link view shows *shape*; the matrix shows *density* and scales better.

# Layouts: where the positions come from {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Where do the node positions come from?

In every chart you've made so far, **position encoded data**: x was a variable, y was a variable.

In a node–link diagram, position comes from a **layout algorithm**.

::: {.gw-box}
The same graph can be drawn in many different ways. The layout is a choice you make, and different choices lead the reader to different conclusions.
:::

## One graph, three layouts

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.6))
layouts = [
    (nx.spring_layout(G, seed=42), "Force-directed (spring)"),
    (nx.circular_layout(G), "Circular"),
    (nx.random_layout(G, seed=1), "Random"),
]
for ax, (lpos, name) in zip(axes, layouts):
    nx.draw_networkx(G, lpos, ax=ax, with_labels=False,
                     node_color="#2E6E8E", node_size=60, edge_color="#cccccc")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11)
    ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Identical data in all three panels. Only the force-directed layout *suggests* the club's two factions.

## How force-directed layout works (intuition)

- Edges act like **springs** pulling connected nodes together
- All nodes **repel** each other like charged particles
- A physics simulation runs until the system settles

So in the final picture:

- Tightly connected groups end up **near each other**
- Distance ≈ "structural closeness" — **not** a measured quantity
- Different runs give different pictures → **fix the random seed**

# Measuring structure: centrality {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Which nodes matter?

**Centrality** = a family of measures that score how *important* a node is — where "important" depends on the question you're asking:

- Who has the most connections? → **degree**
- Who sits *between* groups? → **betweenness**
- Who can reach everyone fastest? → **closeness**

These give **different answers on the same graph** — choosing one is an analytical decision, not a default.

## Degree: count the connections

The simplest measure: a node's **degree** $k_v$ is its number of edges.
(Directed graphs split this into *in-degree* and *out-degree*.)

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
degd = dict(G.degree())
top2 = sorted(degd, key=degd.get, reverse=True)[:2]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.9))
nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, ax=ax, with_labels=False,
                 node_size=[degd[n]*40 for n in G.nodes()],
                 node_color=["#d9534f" if n in top2 else "#2E6E8E" for n in G.nodes()],
                 edge_color="#dddddd")
for n in top2:
    ax.annotate(f"degree {degd[n]}", pos[n], textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(10, 10), fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_title("Node size = degree. The two red hubs: the instructor and the club president.",
             fontsize=11)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Useful property of this dataset: the two highest-degree nodes are exactly the two people the club split between, so degree alone already finds the people the story is about.
:::

## Betweenness: who bridges?

Intuition first — in this graph, **every** path between the two cliques passes through one node:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
B = nx.barbell_graph(5, 1)
bpos = nx.spring_layout(B, seed=5)
btw_b = nx.betweenness_centrality(B)
bridge = max(btw_b, key=btw_b.get)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
nx.draw_networkx(B, bpos, ax=ax, with_labels=False, node_size=320,
                 node_color=["#d9534f" if n == bridge else "#2E6E8E" for n in B.nodes()],
                 edge_color="#999999")
ax.set_title(f"The bridge (red) lies on every inter-group shortest path — betweenness = {btw_b[bridge]:.2f}",
             fontsize=11)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Removing that node disconnects the two halves. It is both a **broker**, because information must pass through it, and a **bottleneck**, for the same reason.

## Betweenness: how it's computed {.smaller}

$$C_B(v) \;=\; \sum_{s \neq v \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}}$$

In words:

1. Take every pair of nodes $(s, t)$
2. Find all **shortest paths** between them ($\sigma_{st}$ of them)
3. Count the fraction that pass **through** $v$
4. Sum over all pairs

::: {.gw-box}
Naïvely this is expensive; in practice **Brandes' algorithm** computes it in roughly $O(N \cdot M)$ for unweighted graphs — and `nx.betweenness_centrality(G)` is one line.
:::

## Closeness: who reaches everyone fastest? {.smaller}

$$C_C(v) \;=\; \frac{N - 1}{\sum_{u \neq v} d(v, u)}$$

where $d(v, u)$ is the shortest-path distance. A node with **small total distance** to everyone has **high closeness** — think: best location for spreading information.

Three measures, three different questions:

| Measure | Question | High score means |
|---|---|---|
| Degree | How connected? | A hub |
| Betweenness | How much of a broker? | A bridge / bottleneck |
| Closeness | How reachable is everyone? | A center of gravity |

## The three measures pick different nodes

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
deg_c = nx.degree_centrality(G)
bet_c = nx.betweenness_centrality(G)
clo_c = nx.closeness_centrality(G)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.4))
for ax, (m, name) in zip(axes, [(deg_c, "Degree"), (bet_c, "Betweenness"), (clo_c, "Closeness")]):
    vals = [m[n] for n in G.nodes()]
    nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, ax=ax, with_labels=False,
                     node_color=vals, cmap=plt.cm.viridis,
                     node_size=[v*900 + 30 for v in vals], edge_color="#dddddd")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Same graph, same layout, but a different set of nodes stands out in each panel. Mapping centrality to colour and size is the first time we encode computed **data** onto the network drawing.

## PageRank: importance that flows along edges {.smaller}

Degree counts every link the same. **PageRank** weights a link by how important the node giving it is — which is circular, and solved by iterating until it settles.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
P = nx.DiGraph()
for i in range(1, 6):                      # A is linked by five obscure pages
    P.add_edge(f"o{i}", "A")
for h in ("H1", "H2"):                     # B is linked by only two — but good ones
    P.add_edge(h, "B")
    for j in range(1, 6):
        P.add_edge(f"m{j}", h)

pr = nx.pagerank(P)
ppos = nx.spring_layout(P, seed=8)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.4, 2.5))
nx.draw_networkx(P, ppos, ax=ax, with_labels=True, font_size=7, font_color="white",
                 node_size=[pr[n] * 5200 + 90 for n in P.nodes()],
                 node_color=["#d9534f" if n in ("A", "B") else "#2E6E8E" for n in P.nodes()],
                 edge_color="#cccccc", arrows=True, arrowsize=9, width=0.9)
ax.set_title(f"Node size = PageRank.   A: in-degree {P.in_degree('A')}, PR {pr['A']:.3f}   ·   "
             f"B: in-degree {P.in_degree('B')}, PR {pr['B']:.3f}", fontsize=10)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**A** is linked five times, **B** only twice — but B's two come from well-linked pages, and B ranks higher. Counting links and weighting them give different answers.

::: {.gw-box}
Read it as a **random surfer**: follow links at random, occasionally jump to a random page. PageRank is the share of time that walker spends on each node. It needs **direction** — on an undirected graph it reduces to roughly degree.

This is what Google was built on: the web is a graph, and its link structure already records which pages people treat as authoritative. `nx.pagerank(G)` is one line.
:::

# Finding groups: community detection {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## What is a community?

A **community** is a set of nodes with **many edges inside** the group and **few edges to the outside**.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from networkx.algorithms.community import greedy_modularity_communities, modularity
comms = list(greedy_modularity_communities(G))
cmap = {}
for cid, c in enumerate(comms):
    for n in c: cmap[n] = cid
within = [(u, v) for u, v in G.edges() if cmap[u] == cmap[v]]
between = [(u, v) for u, v in G.edges() if cmap[u] != cmap[v]]
Q = modularity(G, comms)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.9))
nx.draw_networkx_nodes(G, pos, ax=ax, node_color=[cmap[n] for n in G.nodes()],
                       cmap=plt.cm.Set2, node_size=140)
nx.draw_networkx_edges(G, pos, ax=ax, edgelist=within, edge_color="#2E6E8E", width=1.6)
nx.draw_networkx_edges(G, pos, ax=ax, edgelist=between, edge_color="#bbbbbb", style="dashed")
ax.set_title(f"{len(within)} edges within communities (teal) · {len(between)} between (dashed) · Q = {Q:.2f}",
             fontsize=11)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

No labels were used — the algorithm found the factions **from structure alone**.

## Modularity: scoring a grouping {.smaller}

How do we know a proposed grouping is good? **Modularity**:

$$Q \;=\; \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{ij} \left[ A_{ij} - \frac{k_i k_j}{2m} \right] \delta(c_i, c_j)$$

In plain words:

$$Q \;=\; (\text{fraction of edges inside communities}) \;-\; (\text{expected fraction if edges were random})$$

- $Q \approx 0$: no better than random
- $Q \gtrsim 0.3$: meaningful community structure
- Our karate-club grouping: $Q = 0.41$ ✓

## The algorithm we used: greedy modularity {.smaller}

**Clauset–Newman–Moore (greedy modularity)** — what `greedy_modularity_communities()` runs:

1. Start: every node is its **own** community
2. Find the **pair of communities** whose merge increases $Q$ the most
3. Merge them; repeat
4. Stop when **no merge improves** $Q$

::: {.gw-box}
Worth knowing: **Louvain** (and its successor **Leiden**) follow the same modularity-maximization idea but scale to millions of nodes — the default choice in practice. All are *heuristics*: community detection has no single "correct" answer.
:::

## A different definition: Infomap and the map equation {.smaller}

Greedy modularity, Louvain and Leiden all maximize the **same** objective. **Infomap** optimizes a different one, so it can return a different answer on the same graph.

| | Modularity methods | Infomap |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | More edges inside groups than chance predicts | Shortest description of a random walk |
| Question asked | Where is the graph denser than expected? | Where does flow get trapped? |
| Direction | Usually ignored | Used — flow has a direction |

The idea behind the **map equation**: let a random walker loose on the network and describe its path. If the walker stays inside a group for a long time, you can use short local names inside that group and save space. The grouping that **compresses the walk best** is the one Infomap reports.

::: {.gw-box}
Worth knowing: modularity has a **resolution limit** — below a size that depends on the number of edges, small groups get absorbed into larger ones no matter how clearly separated they are. Flow-based methods are less affected by it.

Try it in the browser at [mapequation.org/apps](https://www.mapequation.org/apps/) — the Infomap app takes a network and shows the partition interactively. It is a separate package (`pip install infomap`), not part of networkx.
:::

## Encoding structure onto the drawing

The layout consumed x/y. The remaining channels carry **computed structure**:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.1))
nx.draw_networkx(G, pos, ax=ax, with_labels=False,
                 node_size=[degd[n]*45 for n in G.nodes()],
                 node_color=[cmap[n] for n in G.nodes()],
                 cmap=plt.cm.Set2, edge_color="#dddddd")
ax.set_title("Size = degree · Colour = detected community",
             fontsize=11)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Hubs, factions and bridges can now all be read off a single picture.

# When the picture fails {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The hairball problem

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
H = nx.barabasi_albert_graph(450, 3, seed=7)
hpos = nx.spring_layout(H, seed=7)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.2))
nx.draw_networkx(H, hpos, ax=ax, with_labels=False,
                 node_color="#2E6E8E", node_size=14,
                 edge_color="#bbbbbb", width=0.4, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_title("450 nodes, about 1,340 edges", fontsize=11)
ax.axis("off"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Node–link diagrams stop being readable somewhere in the **hundreds of nodes**. Adding more of the network to the picture does not add more information for the reader.

## Escaping the hairball {.smaller}

- **Filter** — show a subgraph that matters (top-k by centrality, one community)
- **Aggregate** — collapse communities into super-nodes
- **Switch representations** — adjacency matrix, arc diagram, edge bundling
- **Add interaction** — zoom, hover, select (PyVis → Streamlit, in Block 3)

::: {.gw-box}
Decide what question the picture has to answer, then show the part of the network that answers it. Today's measures are themselves the filters: "the top 20 nodes by betweenness" is a defensible subgraph, chosen for a reason you can state.
:::

## Aggregation, worked on the same hairball {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
hcomms = list(greedy_modularity_communities(H))
hcid = {n: i for i, c in enumerate(hcomms) for n in c}

# Collapse each community to one node. Node size = how many members it has,
# edge width = how many original edges run between the two communities.
Qg = nx.Graph()
for i, c in enumerate(hcomms):
    Qg.add_node(i, members=len(c))
for u, v in H.edges():
    a, b = hcid[u], hcid[v]
    if a != b:
        Qg.add_edge(a, b, weight=Qg.get_edge_data(a, b, {}).get("weight", 0) + 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.2))
nx.draw_networkx(H, hpos, ax=axes[0], with_labels=False, node_color="#2E6E8E",
                 node_size=12, edge_color="#cccccc", width=0.3, alpha=0.7)
axes[0].set_title(f"{H.number_of_nodes()} nodes as drawn before", fontsize=10)
axes[0].axis("off")

qpos = nx.spring_layout(Qg, seed=2)
nx.draw_networkx(Qg, qpos, ax=axes[1], with_labels=False,
                 node_color="#2E6E8E",
                 node_size=[Qg.nodes[n]["members"] * 14 for n in Qg.nodes()],
                 edge_color="#888888",
                 width=[Qg[u][v]["weight"] * 0.12 for u, v in Qg.edges()])
axes[1].set_title(f"{Qg.number_of_nodes()} communities, sized by membership", fontsize=10)
axes[1].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Same network, same edges. The right panel keeps one node per **community** instead of one per member, sizes it by how many members it has, and draws the between-community edges with a width proportional to how many original edges they stand for.

::: {.gw-box}
What you gain is a picture that stays readable as the network grows. What you give up is the individual: no single node can be found on the right. State which one you are showing — an aggregated network answers questions about groups, not about people.
:::

## Interaction, worked on the karate club {.smaller}

```{=html}
<iframe src="../weekly/week6/karate_network.html" width="100%" height="410"
        style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" loading="lazy"
        title="Interactive karate club network"></iframe>
```

Same graph, same encodings — size is degree, colour is community — but the force simulation is running here rather than having been run once and saved as an image.

**Drag a node** and the springs pull its neighbours with it. Hover for degree and community; scroll to zoom. Interaction lets a reader ask one question at a time. You build one of these with PyVis in Block 3.

**3.** Degree, betweenness, and closeness picked different "important" nodes. For a disease-spread network, which matters most? For an org chart?
